segments.text: The first Marathi word — and the everyday greeting of Maharashtra.

(If you already read Devanagari, skim this.) Devanagari runs left to right; every consonant carries a built-in "a." न na, म ma, का kā, र ra. The stroke under स् (a halant) removes its vowel, so the bare s leans onto the next as a conjunct: स् + का becomes स्का. Read न, म, स्, का, र becomes namaskār.

नमस्कार (namaskār) = नमः (namaḥ, "a bow") + कार (kāra, "the making of"), from Sanskrit — literally "the making of a bow." The same word Kannada and Telugu borrowed, and close kin to Hindi's namaskār. But note: where Hindi leans on namaste, Marathi's default, all-purpose greeting is namaskār — one of many small ways the two Devanagari languages differ.
Said with palms pressed together, respectful and neutral — hello and goodbye, any time, to almost anyone. Warmer and more casual: kāy mhaṇtā? ("what do you say?" ≈ "how's it going?") among friends.

segments.text: The formal "thanks" — Sanskrit, shared across the Indian languages.
(Skim if you read Devanagari.) New: ध dha (a breathy d), य ya, वा vā, द da, and the conjunct न्य (na + ya). Read ध, न्य, वा, द becomes dhanyavād.

धन्यवाद (dhanyavād) = Sanskrit dhanya ("worthy") + vāda ("a saying") — "an utterance of '[you are] worthy.'" The same Sanskrit word behind Hindi dhanyavād, Kannada dhanyavāda, Telugu dhanyavādamulu. Warmer, more spoken Marathi often says आभारी आहे (ābhārī āhe, "[I] am grateful"), on the root ābhār, "gratitude."

segments.text: A one-syllable "yes."
(Skim if you read Devanagari.) ह (ha) + the o-mātrā ो becomes हो (ho).

हो (ho, "yes") is Marathi's plain affirmative — distinct from Hindi's hāṁ. Marathi builds its own everyday words on shared Indo-Aryan roots. The polite, fuller "yes" is ho, baraṃ āhe ("yes, it's fine").

segments.text: The partner of ho — built on one of the oldest words in the whole Indo-European family.
(Skim if you read Devanagari.) ना (nā) + ही (hī) becomes nāhī.

नाही (nāhī, "no / is not") sits on the ancient negative na- — the same Proto-Indo-European ne behind English no, not, none, Latin non, and Hindi nahīṁ. So Marathi's "no" and English's "no" are cousins from before either language existed. It doubles as "there isn't": Marathi, like Hindi, denies with this one word.

segments.text: The verbal shrug of Marathi — "sure, fine, all right."
(Skim if you read Devanagari.) ब (ba) + रं (ra with the anusvāra dot ं, a light nasal) becomes baraṃ. That dot on top nasalises the vowel.

बरं (baraṃ, "okay, fine, good, all right") is the oil of everyday Marathi talk — a soft "sure, fine." Its neutral form is bare. A genuinely Marathi word, not a Sanskrit loan — the kind of small, high-frequency word that gives a language its everyday texture.
What does बरं mean, and what does the dot ं do? ("Okay/fine"; the anusvāra nasalises the vowel.)

segments.text: The Marathi goodbye — which, like the Dravidian languages, refuses to say a bare "I'm leaving." And it changes with the speaker's gender.
(Skim if you read Devanagari.) ये (ye) + तो (to) becomes yeto; ये + ते (te) becomes yete.

Marathi, like the Dravidian languages to its south, will not say a bare "I'm leaving." The everyday goodbye is येतो (yeto) — literally "I come [again]," a promise of return, never a final departure. (Fuller: yeto, namaskār.)

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: Marathi verbs carry gender

segments.text: yeto is what a man says; a woman says येते (yete). The verb itself changes with the speaker's gender — something Hindi does only in the past tense, but Marathi does in the present too. (And Marathi keeps three genders — masculine, feminine, and neuter — where Hindi kept only two.) You'll meet this at every verb.

blocks.title: What makes Marathi its own language (not Hindi in Devanagari)

segments.text: It prefers namaskār as the everyday greeting (Hindi leans on namaste).
It keeps three genders — masculine, feminine, neuter — where Hindi kept two.
It marks gender on the verb, even in the present: yeto (m.) / yete (f.).
It has an extra letter, ळ (retroflex ḷ), shared with the Dravidian south and absent from Hindi.
Shared with Hindi/Sanskrit: the Devanagari script, the negative nā- ( from PIE ne, English no), and much formal vocabulary (dhanyavād).
